scenes.title: Gap Analysis
scenes.narration: Gap analysis, also called gaps and islands, finds the missing values and the contiguous runs inside an ordered sequence.

scenes.title: Gaps and islands defined
bullets: An island is a run of consecutive present values
A gap is a stretch of missing values between islands
You may want to list the gaps, or collapse each island into a range
Common uses: missing invoice numbers, absent dates, sensor dropouts
scenes.narration: The problem has two sides. An island is a run of consecutive values that are present, and a gap is the stretch of missing values between two islands. Sometimes you want to report the gaps, such as which invoice numbers are missing, and sometimes you want to collapse each island into a compact start-to-end range. It shows up in missing invoice numbers, absent calendar dates, and gaps in sensor readings.

scenes.title: The row_number difference trick
steps: Assign ROW_NUMBER over the ordered values
Subtract the row number from the value itself
Within a consecutive run, that difference stays constant
Group by the difference to collapse each island
scenes.narration: The classic technique is the row-number difference trick. First, number the rows in order with ROW_NUMBER. Then subtract that row number from the value. Here is the magic: inside a run of consecutive values, the value and the row number increase in lockstep, so their difference is constant. That constant becomes an island identifier, and grouping by it collapses each contiguous run into a single group.

scenes.title: Collapsing consecutive ids into islands
scenes.code:
WITH grouped AS (
    SELECT
        id,
        id - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY id) AS grp
    FROM readings
)
SELECT
    MIN(id) AS island_start,
    MAX(id) AS island_end,
    COUNT(*) AS length
FROM grouped
GROUP BY grp
ORDER BY island_start;
scenes.narration: This collapses runs of consecutive ids into islands. In the CTE, for each id we compute id minus its row number, giving the constant group key described earlier. Consecutive ids share the same key, while a break in the sequence shifts the key. In the outer query we group by that key and take the minimum and maximum id, which are the start and end of each island, plus the count for its length.

scenes.title: Finding the missing dates
scenes.code:
WITH expected AS (
    SELECT generate_series(
        (SELECT MIN(activity_date) FROM daily_activity),
        (SELECT MAX(activity_date) FROM daily_activity),
        INTERVAL '1 day'
    )::date AS d
)
SELECT e.d AS missing_date
FROM expected e
LEFT JOIN daily_activity a
    ON a.activity_date = e.d
WHERE a.activity_date IS NULL
ORDER BY e.d;
scenes.narration: To find gaps directly, we generate the complete sequence we expect and see what is absent. Here generate_series builds every calendar date from the earliest to the latest activity date. We left join the actual activity onto that full calendar, and the rows where the join finds no match, where activity date is null, are exactly the dates with no activity. That gives us a clean list of the missing days.

scenes.text: The value-minus-row-number trick turns 'find contiguous runs' into a simple GROUP BY. It is the single most useful pattern for gaps-and-islands problems.
scenes.narration: The pattern worth memorizing is that subtracting the row number from the value turns finding contiguous runs into a simple GROUP BY, which is the heart of every gaps-and-islands solution.
